narrative.what_i_did: The operator asked for the README to be redesigned so it represents the vision, ultra snazzy, with the thesis out in front. The README was two lines. It was accurate but it was written for a carpenter who already had all the context, not for the sovereignty-curious stranger who lands on the repo from a Nostr link. So this session turned the README into the front door of the project rather than a label on the box.
narrative.whats_pending:
The README is a snapshot and snapshots go stale, which is exactly what happened to STATUS.md. The verified counts sit in three places now: the README, STATUS.md, and .test-baseline.json, and nothing mechanically keeps them agreeing. If the operator wants that to stop drifting, the honest fix is doctrine number four, mechanism over prose: a small check that reads the actual counts and fails when a doc claims something the repo does not support. That is a real cut, not a paragraph, and it was outside what was asked for today so it was not built.

STATUS.md itself is still stale on its own numbers. It says twenty-four feature folders and five hundred thirty-one tests; the repo at HEAD has thirty-two folders and nine hundred three tests. This session did not rewrite STATUS.md because the operator asked for the README and widening the cut unasked is how a small job becomes an unreviewable one. It is worth a five-minute pass in a later session.

The repo also has no LICENSE file. For something offered as a gift to anyone who hits the same walls, that is a real gap and a directional question for the operator rather than a carpenter's choice.
narrative.what_you_could_do_better:
The first draft of the badge row shipped a genuine bug: a shields.io URL containing raw parentheses, which closes a markdown image early and would have rendered as broken text at the very top of the repo's front page. It was caught by re-reading the file rather than by any check, which is luck dressed up as diligence. The lesson taken was to validate rather than eyeball, which is why the mermaid diagrams were then actually parsed rather than assumed good.

The more useful piece of self-criticism is about the numbers. The instinct was to lift the counts from STATUS.md, which is a well-written audit doc that reads authoritative. It was wrong by a third. Running the suite took under a minute and turned a plausible claim into a verified one. Documentation is exactly where unverified numbers go to become permanent, because nothing ever fails when a README lies.

One honest caveat on a number that did ship: the test count of nine hundred three is what vitest actually executes, while the baseline script counts nine hundred by static parse. Both are correct measures of different things. The executed count was used because that is what a reader means by tests passing.
narrative.bigger_picture:
The mission section of CLAUDE.md says the product is the bridge and the education, and that a cut which makes a capability reachable without leaving the person more able to have chosen it themselves is half done. A README is a strange place to notice that rule biting, but it does. For most people who ever encounter this project, the README is the entire product experience. They will never install it. If the README only lists features, it made the project legible and taught nothing, which is the half-done case exactly.

So the structure was built to teach in the same order the wallet teaches: first the inversion, because a person cannot want sovereignty until they see that they currently rent their identity; then the one primitive, because the genesis key and the succession chain and the Merkle field tree are the whole idea and everything else is composition; then what actually ships, so the thesis is not mistaken for a manifesto. The line about identity being the attestations rather than the key was put at the very bottom deliberately, because it is the idea that reframes losing your seed from erasure into inconvenience, and it lands better after the reader has seen the machinery that makes it true.

There is a thread here that connects to priority four on the STATUS list, the verification page as a teaching surface. That cut and this one are the same instinct pointed at two different strangers: one who arrives at the repo and one who arrives at a proof. Both currently get shown a result and told to trust it. Both should be walked through why the math is real. The README is the cheaper half of that pair and it is now done, which makes the verify-page cut easier to argue for because the voice already exists to copy.

operator_directives: "Can you redesign the tapit wallet repo read me to represent our vision. Make it ultra snazzy and get our thesis out there." -- read as a public-facing rewrite aimed at a stranger, not an internal status doc. Snazzy was taken to mean visually strong on GitHub specifically (centered hero, badges, mermaid diagrams, comparison tables) rather than merely verbose.
next_session_starts_with: Ground against README.md as it now stands, since it is the public statement of the thesis and any future claim about the project should agree with it. Two follow-ups are worth surfacing to the operator as a chip-form question: whether to add a LICENSE (the mission frames the wallet as a gift, and there is no license file, so the default is all-rights-reserved which contradicts the framing), and whether to spend a session on the counts-drift check described in whats_pending. If neither is wanted, the highest-leverage cut remains unchanged: the release-ceremony UX sub-cut D1, the operator request surface.
feedback_to_appcommander: Two things worth lifting. First, STATUS.md drifted by roughly a third on its headline counts while reading completely authoritative, and a carpenter under time pressure will believe it. Any spawn that keeps a status doc with numbers in it should either generate those numbers or have a check that fails when they diverge; this is a fleet-wide instance of doctrine four, mechanism over prose. Second, the fresh-clone test path has a sharp edge: three test files fail to resolve until the local file: dependencies are built, because only prebuild builds them. A newcomer running npm test first sees three red files and reasonably concludes the repo is broken. Either wire a pretest that builds the local packages, or say so in the README, which is what was done here as the cheaper fix.
